title: Know It Cold
author: Chris O'Brien
summary: O'Brien argues that most schoolwide instructional improvement fails because principals build fragments (a coaching cycle here, a walkthrough tool there) rather than a connected instructional system. He lays out eight subsystems, from vision and training through lesson preparation, live feedback, PD, data meetings, intervention and interim assessment, and names a failure mode and a diagnostic question for each. His through-line is that every subsystem has a precondition that lives in the leader: the principal must know the work cold enough to lead each piece personally. Without that, he says, the leader is doing instructional management, not instructional leadership. He closes with a story of a teacher he coached intensively who wanted more coaching than she could get, offered as the standard to aim for.
points: Fragments such as a coaching cycle with no vision behind it look like instructional leadership but produce activity, not schoolwide change.
The eight-subsystem model runs from vision to interim assessment, and breaking the sequence anywhere damages everything downstream.
Lesson preparation and rehearsal with the teacher, before the lesson, is the most skipped subsystem and the highest-leverage one.
Live, in-the-moment feedback tied to an already-trained target beats delayed batch feedback and vague abstractions like rigor or engagement.
Data meetings only matter if they run the full chain to a scheduled reteach, and PD topics should come from walkthrough data rather than the district calendar.
quotes: Each fragment looks like instructional leadership in isolation. None of them produce schoolwide change because none of them are wired to the others.
The vision is specific enough that two teachers in adjacent rooms produce recognizably aligned instruction. Jargon-free enough that a new teacher can describe it without consulting a document.
Most schools confuse training with onboarding. They run a week in August and call the work done. Then they wonder why year-three teachers run the same instructional block in visibly different ways.
Most teachers were never taught to prepare a lesson to the standard the work requires. Teacher prep programs focus on classroom management and lesson structure.
Live feedback happens at the point of error. The whisper during independent practice. The forty-five-second prompt in a doorway.
Most data meetings produce exactly that. Teachers gather, look at scores, identify struggling students, discuss interventions in general terms, and leave. Nothing about instruction has changed.
If you do not, the work you are doing is not instructional leadership. It is instructional management. The two are not the same thing and they do not produce the same outcomes.
